extracted.intended_audience: academic authors submitting manuscripts to peer-reviewed journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on submitting manuscripts to journals, responding to peer review, handling rejection, and managing post-acceptance tasks (proofs/copyright). Applicable across academic disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible decisions after submission
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three possible outcomes once your article has been submitted: accept, reject or revise. Variations include desk rejection, accept without change, conditional acceptance pending major revision, conditional acceptance with minor revision, and rejection after peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desk rejection is rapid and often for scope/quality reasons; accept without change is very rare; conditional acceptance (major or minor) may lead to further peer review after revision; minor revisions are usually published if made; rejection after peer review is common and requires coping strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desk rejection (editorial rejection without peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Desk rejection: This occurs when an article has been rejected outright by the editor-in-chief, usually without being sent for peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common reasons include not fitting the journal scope, poor English, and poor data analysis (the appendix lists more reasons). To avoid desk rejection seek informal advice before submission (e.g., ask the editor if the manuscript is of interest while still in preparation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide suggested reviewers at submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should suggest appropriate reviewers when submitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest at least 2–5 appropriate reviewers to potentially speed processing and help the editor find referees; this can sometimes reduce the chance of desk rejection by showing reviewer interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address every reviewer comment point-by-point
rubrics_metrics.description: It is crucial that every single comment is addressed to maximise the chance of subsequent publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a detailed point-by-point response letter listing all reviewer comments and your responses. Address even vague or apparently incorrect comments, and provide clear explanations of changes made or reasons for not making changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight changes in the revised manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight any changes that you have made in the manuscript itself so that these changes are apparent and stand out easily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tracked changes or clearly marked edits to help editors and reviewers see revisions quickly; this expedites re-review and demonstrates thoroughness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain and justify disagreements with reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: If you chose not to make a change in response to a specific comment made by the reviewer, you must state the reason why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You are allowed to disagree with a reviewer, but provide a polite, reasoned explanation in the response letter rather than ignoring the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rush the revision process
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rush through the revision process or avoid responding to any points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major rewrites take significant time; consider whether the effort is worthwhile. Rushing can lead to incomplete responses and reduce chances of acceptance; if a major rewrite is not worthwhile, consider submitting elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remain constructive and polite in responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Remain constructive and polite regardless of how irritated you may be by the comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone matters. Politeness and professionalism in replies improve the reception of your rebuttals and revisions; hostile or dismissive responses are counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for multiple rounds of revision
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not uncommon for a journal to request several revisions of an article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that even after one revision your manuscript may be sent back for further changes; plan time and resources accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional major revision may trigger further peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditional acceptance pending major revision: Once the article has been revised, it may be sent out for peer review again to the same or different reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no guarantee of acceptance after major revision, though chances may be higher. Thorough, well-documented revisions reduce risk of further rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling rejection: appeal only with compelling grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: If you feel that the comments were grossly unfair or wrong, consider writing to the editor and request an appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals are rarely successful and you usually have only one chance. The editor might send the article for further review, but this is unlikely unless you present a compelling argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling rejection: resubmit elsewhere and incorporate criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Send your article to another journal. Maximise the chances of publication elsewhere by focusing on any comments and incorporating these into your article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reviewer feedback to improve the manuscript before resubmission. Be aware the same referee might see the revised paper at a different journal; failing to address prior comments risks immediate rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling rejection: abandon if research is invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: Give up on the article. It is possible that there is a methodological or data problem with your article that invalidates the research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the study is fundamentally flawed, publishing could harm your reputation. Recognise when the correct action is to stop pursuing publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request editorial feedback when no reviewer comments provided
rubrics_metrics.description: If no feedback was received with the decision letter, there may be editorial marks on the returned manuscript. If not, ask the editor-in-chief for feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume silence means quality or poor quality. Soliciting feedback can clarify reasons for rejection and guide improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-acceptance duties: respond to copy-edit queries and proof corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a journal has accepted your article, it will be copy-edited, typeset and you will be sent a PDF proof accompanied by queries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to every proof query (e.g., missing references, sentence clarifications, dates websites were accessed). The PDF proof is the final chance for corrections — check tables, illustrations and units of measurement carefully. Deadlines can be tight (as short as 48 hours).

rubrics_metrics.name: Return signed copyright agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher may send a copyright agreement with the proof, which must be returned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals are unlikely to publish without a signed copyright agreement; return it together with your corrected proof to avoid publication delays.
